item.title: Manhunt Begins After Convicted Murderer Escapes From Tennessee Prison
item.description:
A manhunt was underway on Monday for an inmate who had escaped from a correctional facility in Tennessee, where he was serving a life sentence for murder, officials said.

The man, Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was discovered to be missing around 11:30 p.m. on Sunday at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tenn., about 125 miles north of Memphis, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement Monday morning.

The New York Times

Staff members immediately searched the prison, the statement said. A review of the security cameras showed Mr. Morley had breached the complex’s perimeter fence and fled in his prison uniform, officials said.

The department said it was working with local, state and federal law enforcement officials to find Mr. Morley. Buildings and structures near the prison have been searched and cleared, officials said. The Tennessee Highway Patrol deployed aerial support and state troopers to assist with the search, the department said.

Mr. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder in 2025 in the death of Cody Birchfield, who had been reported missing in February 2022, according to the TV news station WJHL in Johnson City, Tenn.

Mr. Morley was arrested in North Carolina in March 2022. WJHL reported that after he was taken into custody, deputies searched Mr. Morley’s home and found Mr. Birchfield’s body there.

Prison records show Mr. Morley had also been convicted of aggravated burglary and tampering with evidence. Records also show that Mr. Morley was convicted of evading arrest in 2022 and of vandalism in 2024.

He was added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation’s Most Wanted list after his escape, the corrections department said. Officials are offering a reward of up to $2,500 for information leading to Mr. Morley’s arrest.

item.title: Bob Woodward Thought Jeff Bezos Had His Back. Now He Feels Disillusioned.
item.description:
When Bob Woodward, the veteran star Washington Post reporter of Watergate fame, was about to publish a hard-hitting book about President Trump in 2018, he called the owner of his newspaper, Jeff Bezos, to warn him.

“Don’t worry, I have your back, Bob,” Mr. Bezos told him. “I’ll always have your back.”

“Always” turned out not to be as long as it used to be, Mr. Woodward now says he discovered. After more than a half-century breaking stories about Washington, one of the scoops in Mr. Woodward’s new memoir is his own breakup in all but name with Mr. Bezos, who in his view turned out to not have the backs of the journalists working for him, after all.

Instead, Mr. Woodward writes, Mr. Bezos has been “compromising public trust in The Washington Post’s aggressive and independent journalism” in deference to Mr. Trump. While he says Mr. Bezos has not interfered in news stories, Mr. Woodward writes that the billionaire owner’s sweeping staff cuts, reorientation of the editorial page and personal ingratiation to the president have betrayed the legacy of a newspaper known for courageous coverage.

The condemnation of Mr. Bezos by his most famous employee is one of the headlines from “Secrets,” the long-awaited memoir of his 55 years in journalism to be published Nov. 24 by Mr. Woodward, who still holds the title of associate editor at the paper.

A copy of the memoir was obtained by The New York Times. Here are six takeaways:

For decades, Mr. Woodward guarded the identity of the sources of his blockbuster stories and best selling books. But now, he finally names names. Many of his early sources have died, and he received permission from others still alive to identify them.

While W. Mark Felt, the former deputy F.B.I. director, unmasked himself in 2005 as the famous Watergate source called Deep Throat, much of Washington will pore through this new book to learn who else talked. It turns out that lots of people did, including presidents, cabinet secretaries, generals, spymasters, Supreme Court justices and F.B.I. agents.

Mr. Woodward discloses for the first time his sources for one of the most iconic scenes he ever reported, a moment shortly before Richard M. Nixon resigned because of Watergate, when the sobbing president asked Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger to fall to his knees and pray with him.

The sources, the book now reveals, were two of Mr. Kissinger’s lieutenants, Brent Scowcroft and Lawrence S. Eagleburger. While neither was present for the scene, Mr. Kissinger described it to them shortly afterward and the two then listened in on the phone when Mr. Nixon called Mr. Kissinger to ask him not to tell anyone he had cried.

Mr. Woodward also describes lengthy conversations with two of Mr. Nixon’s own lawyers, J. Fred Buzhardt Jr. and Leonard Garment, neither of whom seemed to hold their client in high regard. “He flat out lies,” Mr. Buzhardt told Mr. Woodward. Mr. Garment separately told Mr. Woodward that Mr. Nixon was “a very strange man, very strange” and “guilty of misdemeanors.” By not destroying his secret Oval Office tapes, Mr. Nixon was “letting America into the toilet of his mind,” Mr. Garment said. “The impeachable offense was letting us all see.”

The new memoir also describes Mr. Woodward’s closeness with Richard G. Darman, a key Republican official under multiple presidents who became both one of his best sources and best friends. As excerpted in The New Yorker, the conflict ultimately led to a rupture after Mr. Woodward published a harsh series on President George H.W. Bush’s economic policies shortly before the 1992 election, based in part on Mr. Darman’s descriptions.

One of Mr. Woodward’s earliest books was “The Brethren,” a penetrating look inside the normally secretive chambers of the Supreme Court, written with Scott Armstrong, that stunned the legal world and beyond. For years, lawyers and judges wondered how Mr. Woodward got inside one of the most tightly guarded institutions in Washington.

In “Secrets,” Mr. Woodward discloses the names of five justices who spoke with the authors, all of whom have since died: Potter Stewart, Lewis F. Powell Jr., Byron R. White, Harry A. Blackmun and William H. Rehnquist. And he describes how he obtained one of the documents that informed the book: a secret history of the Nixon Watergate tapes case, which revealed the internal debate among the justices over how to rule.

He went to the home of Steven P. Goldberg, who was a clerk to Justice William J. Brennan Jr. and had authored the case history, but refused to give it to Mr. Woodward. The reporter convinced him to instead read it to him, which Mr. Goldberg proceeded to do. But it was long and Mr. Woodward took his time scribbling down notes. Finally, an exhausted Mr. Goldberg nodded off.

Mr. Woodward waited 20 minutes so that Mr. Goldberg would reach a deep sleep. He decided not to simply take the document — “that seemed a little too far, even for me” — so he nudged Mr. Goldberg and simply told him that he would borrow it and bring it back the next morning. The groggy clerk stirred and mumbled his assent. Mr. Woodward wrote that he did his best not to race out the door with the document. “If I was on a security camera I wanted to be behaving properly, with whatever might be left of my dignity,” he writes.

Mr. Woodward also writes about encounters with more recent justices. He reports that his wife, Elsa Walsh, a former journalist for The Post and The New Yorker, sat next to former Justice Stephen G. Breyer at a dinner and he told her that he was “forced out” to make way for someone younger on the court.

He also recalls running into Justice Elena Kagan at a Washington party in 2023. Justice Kagan expressed admiration for “The Brethren” and Mr. Woodward noted that the main point was how the ideological center of the court in that era dominated. “Yes, I prefer it that way,” Justice Kagan said. “That’s exactly what it should be.”

When he asked her if she was happy on the court, Justice Kagan said no, she was not, given the situation.

For all his fame, Mr. Woodward is known in Washington as something of a closed door himself. He loves talking about reporting and politics, but has generally been reticent about his personal life. While this book, his 24th, is not exactly an exercise in introspection, at age 83 he finally opens up at least a bit more than he has done in public.

He recounts growing up in a broken home in Wheaton, Ill. He caught his mother kissing another man and then discovered that his parents were getting divorced when he rummaged through his father’s sock drawer and found a private letter. He writes that he “learned at a very young age the pain of secrets and how they can destroy lives and started down a path of trying to find them.”

Mr. Woodward also writes that a fire gutted his home as a child, leaving him so anxious to this day that he keeps multiple fire extinguishers throughout his Washington home. He describes finding a way as a young Navy officer to get out of a deployment to Vietnam, only to learn later that the man who went instead ended up dying. And he recalls falling out with his Watergate partner Carl Bernstein during the writing of their second book, “The Final Days,” and how it took years to repair the friendship.

Mr. Woodward addresses some of the controversies of his career. He insists that, despite denials and doubts, he did get into a hospital room to see a dying William J. Casey, the C.I.A. director in the 1980s — he was let in, he writes, by a security agent he had befriended. He publishes images of the notes that he took quoting Mr. Casey acknowledging a role in the Iran-contra affair by saying, “I believed.”

By contrast, he accepts blame for “my spectacular failure” as an editor in publishing a fabricated story by the Post reporter Janet Cooke about what turned out to be a fictional 8-year-old heroin addict. That incident convinced him “that I was not cut out to be an editor.”

One of the other mistakes in judgment Mr. Woodward acknowledges was his faith in Mr. Bezos. “I remember feeling relief when Jeff decided to buy The Post in 2013,” he writes. “I believed at the time that Bezos would provide the finances for The Post to continue to operate courageously.”

But his views began to change in 2024, when Mr. Bezos decided just before the election to pull an endorsement of Kamala Harris and declare that The Post would no longer endorse presidential candidates. “At the time, I thought, is he not reading his own newspaper or my books about Trump?” Mr. Woodward writes. The timing made it look “like Bezos and the newspaper were capitulating to Trump.”

Mr. Bezos then shifted the opinion pages to only advocate “personal liberties and free markets” with no dissenting views. “I could only imagine the agony this kind of decision would have caused Kay or Ben,” he adds, referring to Katharine Graham and Benjamin C. Bradlee, the publisher and executive editor during Watergate.

He came to believe that the “benefit of the doubt” that he had given Mr. Bezos was unwarranted. While he notes that The Post continues to produce aggressive coverage of Mr. Trump, Mr. Woodward laments that Mr. Bezos has not publicly defended independent journalism against the president’s campaign of intimidation the way that A.G. Sulzberger, publisher of The Times, has. “It pains me that Jeff Bezos has remained silent,” he writes. “It is not too late for media owners to prioritize moral courage over financial gain.”

A representative of Mr. Bezos did not respond to a request for comment. Matt Murray, The Post’s executive editor, said that he appreciated Mr. Woodward’s praise for the paper’s recent coverage and added that Mr. Bezos had never interfered in news reporting.

“With Jeff’s backing, the company is getting back in shape and poised for our best decade,” he said in a statement. “More than that, the Woodwards and Bernsteins of today are breaking consequential stories that have people talking about us in a way they haven’t in years, with total independence and encouragement from our owner.”

item.title: Judge Temporarily Blocks Further Alterations at D.C.’s East Potomac Park
item.description:
A federal judge temporarily barred the Interior Department on Monday from carrying out a variety of major alterations at East Potomac Park, finding that the government had been taking steps to initiate President Trump’s vision for a championship-level golf course on the property while passing off the work in court as routine maintenance.

The ruling followed a confrontation between the Justice Department and Judge Ana C. Reyes, who throughout October called several Trump administration officials and government lawyers to account for what she described as misrepresentations about the plan.

The clash underscored what had been one of the president’s less visible plans for transforming the capital, compared to his efforts to seize control of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and add a gilded ballroom to the White House. This, instead, was the overhaul of a municipal golf course and public park.

It culminated in a searing 70-page opinion issued on Monday, in which Judge Reyes wrote that much of what she had been told in court stood at odds with Mr. Trump’s public pronouncements about the golf course, which came even as officials were insisting that no long-term plan was settled.

“Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president,” she wrote. “Not to believe him that a cabinet secretary has ‘developed’ a federal land project. Not to believe him that the secretary’s agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land.”

“And yet, here we are,” she added.

Mr. Trump railed against the ruling on social media late Monday, saying the course would be closed as scheduled. He vowed to “immediately appeal” the decision.

“The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” he wrote. “We are asking the D.C. Circuit Court for immediate remedy.”

Judge Reyes marveled that a local dispute over a golf course had spiraled into a broader examination of the Trump administration’s tactics, requiring judges to anticipate when and where the federal government might abruptly move to carry out the president’s personal goals and projects.

“It now forces the court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys,” she wrote. “This morass of different accounts concerns the future of the East Potomac Golf Course, a historic landmark.”

A group that included two Washington residents and a preservation society that sued to block an overhaul of the existing site had asked the court to prevent the administration from cutting down more trees after 400 were felled in one morning earlier this month.

Judge Reyes granted the request and went further, barring other actions that could indirectly destroy trees, including staging heavy machinery. She went to great lengths to impart her instructions in detail, an apparent attempt to prevent the administration from citing confusion or ambiguity to act without her involvement.

She required the government to notify the court at least 10 days before closing the course or making any “irreversible modification to any forms or features” to East Potomac Park, where the current course is, including changes to “the park’s landforms, vegetation, course design, hydrology, pathways, and structures.”

“This is a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm,” said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the group behind the lawsuit.

The dramatic changes that Mr. Trump has made to Washington loomed over the lawsuit from the beginning.

Throughout early interactions with Justice Department attorneys on the case, Judge Reyes stressed that she wanted to avoid surprises, after the president acted without warning last year to demolish the East Wing of the White House before courts could review the legality of the project.

At the same time, she said the lawsuit placed her in a difficult spot, because she did not view it as the role of federal courts to police minor decisions about management of federal lands. While Mr. Trump had mused since last year about transforming plans for East Potomac Park. But earlier this year Judge Reyes repeatedly told the group behind the lawsuit that it was not yet clear that the federal government was implementing his vision, making court action premature.

Hesitant to issue any order that would prevent rank-and-file government workers from carrying out everyday maintenance on the course, she asked the Justice Department to provide early warning before workers started major work at the golf course.

Judge Reyes stressed on Monday that she stood by that approach, and she had not tied the government’s hands more than necessary.

“The events surrounding this case have become extraordinary,” she wrote. “The legal result is not.”

During hearings in May and July, she told government lawyers she expected professionalism and that she would trust them to let her know when plans firmed up and if the government was preparing to begin work on the course Mr. Trump had described.

She stressed she would give the Justice Department “the benefit of the doubt” and that she was confident that workers would not “act first and ask forgiveness later.”

But in October, that calculus changed.

“The government then did precisely what plaintiffs feared,” she wrote in an opinion earlier this month.

On a Friday evening, headed into the Columbus Day weekend, the Justice Department filed an update advising that the Interior Department had crafted a plan to clear hundreds of trees across the course. The next morning, just hours later, the crews arrived and cut them down.

At that point, Judge Reyes rebuked the Justice Department, vowing to get answers about who authorized the cutting, whether it was in preparation for Mr. Trump’s renovation and how much time had passed between the decision to cut down the trees and the Justice Department’s filing alerting the court.

In two hearings, she ordered four Interior Department officials to recount how the decision was made. She sparred with Stanley Woodward Jr., the third most senior official at the Justice Department, who stepped in to represent the government.

In the meantime, Mr. Trump announced in several social media posts in October that work would begin “immediately” and the course would close in November to complete the project.

In the opinion on Monday, Judge Reyes wrote that she found the testimony by most of the relatively junior Interior Department officials credible. But she wrote that Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee serving as deputy chief of staff to Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, did not appear to have honestly disclosed what he knew about the plan to remove trees.

She noted that Mr. Wischer had been photographed carrying design plans for the course while touring the grounds with Mr. Trump and Mr. Burgum in June. She expressed doubt that he “just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management,” as he appeared to suggest when describing in court his role managing the course.

item.title: Obama’s ‘Cheesecake Factory’ Jab Rankles Trump on Mississippi Campaign Stop
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama has struck a nerve with President Trump.

Mr. Trump took time from campaign issues to defend his fixation on remodeling the White House in his second term on Monday after Mr. Obama jabbed that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Mr. Trump spoke for several minutes about the remark on his way to a campaign swing in Mississippi, then delivered an extensive aside there on the White House ballroom, helipad and other projects. He was in the solidly Republican state, which has been shifting toward Democrats, as part of his swing through ruby red America to shore up candidates ahead of the midterms.

Mr. Trump, whose approval ratings are at record lows, at times insisted he had spent “very little time” on redesigning the White House, parts of which he has demolished to make way for the new ballroom. But he also defended his focus on the renovations and eventually conceded that “I have fun doing it.”

“It actually relaxes me,” Mr. Trump said in Corinth, asserting he was actually “fixing up the White House.” He added, to cheers from the supportive crowd, “Isn’t that a nice thing to do?”

Even allies and aides inside the White House have conceded that with the war in Iran grinding on, gas prices at uncomfortable highs and Americans chafing at the rising cost of living, Mr. Trump is finding reprieve by focusing on ornate renovation projects in the nation’s capital, chief among them his effort to remake the White House in his image.

Mr. Obama delivered the Cheesecake Factory attack line at a rally in Ohio on Saturday, casting Mr. Trump as out of touch while needling at the president’s extravagant sense of style. Saddam Hussein, the authoritarian leader of Iraq who was ousted by the 2003 U.S. invasion, was known for his love of gold.

The former president’s remarks sparked Mr. Trump’s most devoted critics and supporters. Trump administration officials and other Republicans responded with indignation, and sought to turn the attack upon Mr. Obama. They asserted the former president was the elitist for taking a swing at the Cheesecake Factory. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, had lunch at a Cheesecake Factory in Washington on Monday, quipping “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.”

No one appeared more insulted than Mr. Trump. In a six-minute gaggle with reporters on his way to Mississippi, the president devoted more than half his speaking time to Mr. Obama’s remarks. He spent comparatively little time repeating his unfounded claims of massive voter fraud.

“For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” Mr. Trump said, before calling Mr. Obama “a stupid person.”

Once onstage, Mr. Trump devoted another six minutes to defending his makeover of the White House, and other parts of the nation’s capital.

“Nobody loved it like I do,” Mr. Trump said of the White House, speaking fondly of beautiful marble and painted columns, and of painstakingly replacing windows and tiles that were in disrepair.

He continued, “We made it all beautiful.”

item.title: A Tight Senate Race in Mississippi? Trump and Others Seem to Think So.
item.description:
Some of the two party’s biggest names, including President Trump and his opponent in 2024, Kamala Harris, have dropped in for rallies. Money is flowing in the millions of dollars. The airwaves are saturated with cutting political ads.

All for a Senate race in Mississippi, one of the most Republican states in the country.

The race between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, an incumbent Republican, and Scott Colom, a district attorney with deep roots in the state, has raised a tantalizing question in the final days of the midterm season: Could Mississippi, a state flickering on the outskirts of the Democratic Party’s wildest ambitions, actually be in play?

Mr. Trump’s rally on Monday night with Ms. Hyde-Smith in Corinth, a short drive from the Tennessee border, seemed to indicate that it might be.

“I’m here because Cindy is doing great,” the president told the packed arena. “But I’ve just got to make sure.”

He went on to Mr. Colom. “How the hell do you say that guy’s name?” he asked, adding, “I don’t have to go into him — he’s a disaster.”

Mr. Colom seemed happy to take the slight. His campaign posted photos showing him at Mr. Trump’s rally talking to voters in line.

“I hope people will realize that Mississippi was always a state that had potential,” Mr. Colom said this month at a cafe in Jackson, the capital. “But it does need resources and attention.”

In a bastion of conservatism, a healthy dose of skepticism is warranted. Democrats here have let their hopes climb in recent years — with Mike Espy, a former agriculture secretary running for Senate, in 2018, and Brandon Presley, a candidate for governor in 2023 — only to see them dashed.

“We’ve seen this movie before,” Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, said in an interview. “I don’t see the doomsday coming on Nov. 3.”

But the flurry of high-profile surrogates and millions of national dollars from the parties’ official political arms, and their leaderships’ super PACs, signal a tightening race if not a tossup.

“He will never outwork me,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said of Mr. Colom during the rally. “I have a proven record to run on that I am very, very proud of.”

Beyond the rallies and star stand-ins, the money is speaking volumes. Some Black Democrats had clamored for the party establishment to invest in Mississippi and the man who would be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Mr. Colom, a relentless messenger, has capitalized on boiling voter anger over high prices, cuts to health care and food assistance and the war in Iran.

With the Senate races in Georgia and North Carolina seeming to shift toward the Democrats, Mississippi appears to be the new front in an expanding battlefield in the South.

That prompted a hefty round of spending from the Senate Majority PAC, which is affiliated with the Senate Democratic leadership. The Senate Leadership Fund, connected to Senate Republicans, has now pumped more than $1 million of advertising into Mississippi, according to AdImpact, which monitors campaign advertising,

“Whether he wins or not, he ran a good race,” Mary Wallace Hodge, 79, a retired store manager in Columbus, Miss., said of Mr. Colom. “Republicans are scared.”

Mr. Colom is the son of a barrier-breaking regional judge and a lawyer who worked on Ronald Reagan’s transition team.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the Senate, has not been as dominant as some of her other Republican counterparts. The state’s former agriculture commissioner, Ms. Hyde-Smith was first appointed to the Senate seat after the 2018 retirement of Senator Thad Cochran, who was adept at bringing federal funds to the state.

The state’s senior senator, Roger Wicker, a Republican, has followed in Mr. Cochran’s footsteps as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Ms. Hyde-Smith has a seat on the panel that controls spending and has taken care in recent days to highlight the money that she has driven home. For some Republicans, that is enough to reliably support Mr. Trump’s agenda.

“He can’t do it by himself,” said Sharon Pannell, 57, a retired teacher who came to the rally in Corinth on Monday. “I think a lot of people don’t know how important the midterm election is.”

But Ms. Hyde-Smith has otherwise kept a low profile, declining questions from the reporters who prowl the Senate basement and refusing to debate Mr. Colom. In Starkville, Miss., one farmer told Mr. Colom that he wouldn’t know what Ms. Hyde-Smith looked like, if not for the fairly recent barrage of TV advertisements.

One of her decisions in the Senate was fateful: She refused to sign off on Mr. Colom’s nomination to the federal judiciary during the Biden administration, effectively blocking his path to the lifetime appointment and leaving him free to challenge her this year.

“I wouldn’t have left the bench to run for the United States Senate, that is fair,” Mr. Colom said. But, he said, his motivation was not personal.

“Mississippi did not matter enough to her,” he said. “Ultimately, that’s the betrayal.”

He has pilloried Ms. Hyde-Smith as “Cindy High Prices” and says she has not done enough for the state. He has worked to build a coalition behind the promise that “Mississippi Matters,” playing off a frustration that the state has struggled to climb national rankings.

Then there’s the protein ad.

In February, after a local TV anchor referenced the high price of beef while asking about the rising costs of food, Ms. Hyde-Smith observed: “You have so many proteins to choose from.”

Eight months later, Mr. Colom dropped a punchy, 30-second ad off the clip. A trio of dumbfounded voters riff on the same response: Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.

It has become the catchphrase on his campaign’s food truck (pick another protein — beef or chicken — for your taco), on campaign posters and even among some voters.

“I’d rather pick another senator,” Kierra Robinson, 33, told Mr. Colom as he knocked on doors in her Jackson neighborhood, quoting the ad back at him in recognition. “I like you.”

An energized Black electorate, which makes up about 40 percent of the state’s population, could lift Mr. Colom but only so far. Former President Barack Obama, whose 2008 campaign prompted a record surge of Black voting, reached about 43 percent that year.

The ongoing effort to redraw districts across the South after the weakening of the Voting Rights Act this year has also helped galvanize many Black voters.

“Mississippi’s not a red state — it’s a state that doesn’t vote,” said Carol Hall, 66, a Southaven, Miss., retiree who had been out canvassing prospective voters for the first time in her life.

But to win, Mr. Colom needs support from more than just Black voters.

Some of those voters seem willing to at least consider him. A young Catholic woman, passionate about her opposition to abortion, said she was looking for a candidate opposed to the data center development near her neighborhood in Horn Lake, Miss., a short drive from Memphis. A gaggle of 18-year-old men spoke about high gas prices and their worries about a protracted conflict in Iran as they debated their first vote.

Roger Keesling said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but came to Mr. Colom’s rally with Ms. Harris earlier this month to learn more about the guy in the ads that popped up during an episode of “The Voice.”

“I’ve been doing my homework on Cindy Hyde-Smith, and I’m not that impressed,” Mr. Keesling said, speaking before the rally. Mr. Colom, he said, seemed like “he works for the people.”

item.title: The ‘Strip Club King’ of Tampa Has Died
item.description:
Joe Redner, the so-called strip club king of Tampa, who became an outspoken champion of a woman’s right to bare it all for paying customers — and, as the years went by, a vocal defender of free speech, gay rights and reproductive freedom — died on Oct. 16 at his home in Tampa, Fla. He was 86.

He had been fighting cancer that had metastasized from his lungs, his son, Joey Redner, said.

During his 50-year career in adult entertainment, Mr. Redner owned an empire of strip clubs in and around Tampa, a longtime hotbed for both adult entertainment and its culturally conservative critics.

But his best-known venue, by far, was Mons Venus, on the city’s west side. After opening in 1982, it immediately became one of the area’s most popular adult venues. Dozens of women could often be found parading on its platforms, all in various states of undress.

The club was a lightning rod for religious groups, which held vigils outside its doors. One paid for a billboard above the club that read, “Forgive them, Father, for they know not what they do.”

Mr. Redner also faced a steady campaign by city politicians, who tried to use zoning regulations and public-nuisance laws to shut him down.

But whenever challenged, he stood his ground. If he knew the police were coming, he made sure to be on the premises so he would be arrested alongside his dancers and patrons. (He claimed to have been thrown in jail 150 times.)

He ran his club in shifts, so that when one set of dancers and employees was taken to jail, another moved quickly into place. If the second set was arrested, a third crew was waiting.

“It was a game — who’s smarter?” he said in the documentary “Strip Club King: The Story of Joe Redner” (2008).

Mr. Redner also fought back in court. He paid his dancers’ and patrons’ legal fees, and his business partner was a bail bondsman, which meant his people could move through the system quickly and be back at the club within a few hours.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Though he had dropped out of high school, he spent years studying First Amendment law and worked closely with his longtime lawyer, Luke Lirot, to oppose city ordinances against nude dancing. On the shelves in his office, law journals shared space with back issues of Playboy.

“He’s at the Tampa law library all day, day after day, week after week, trying to study ways to make the best argument he could make,” Mr. Lirot said in an interview.

A political independent with a strong streak of civil libertarianism, Mr. Redner mounted several campaigns for Tampa City Council, as well as the Hillsborough County Commission and the State Legislature. He never won, but in 2007 he forced a runoff with an incumbent councilwoman, Gwen Miller. (She won, with 56 percent of the vote.)

He ran for office, he said, to fight for others’ rights — not just the rights of adult performers, but those of women, L.G.B.T.Q. people and political protesters.

Mr. Redner fashioned himself as a sort of Sun Belt Diogenes, the Greek cynic, denouncing corruption and hypocrisy in Tampa’s civic leadership. At public hearings, he liked to point out which politicians had visited Mons Venus.

“They say the golf club is where deals get made,” he said in “Strip Club King.” Shaking his head, he added: “It’s the Mons.”

In addition to campaigning at the ballot box, he found other ways to fight. In 2002, he bought a piece of land, landscaped it and opened it to the public as Voice of Freedom Park. A decade later, he allowed members of the local branch of the Occupy movement to camp out there.

In 2003, Mr. Redner was one of several people arrested outside a rally in Tampa where President George W. Bush was speaking.

After the County Commission passed a law forbidding government agencies from expressing support for a local Gay Pride march in 2005, Mr. Redner sued. When the court ruled that he lacked standing because the new law did not affect him, he announced that he was gay (he was not). He still lost the case, but the commission reversed its decision in 2013.

And in 2018, following a cancer diagnosis, Mr. Redner won court approval to grow marijuana for medical use, though 17 days later an appellate court reversed the decision.

“I’m a freedom type of guy,” he told The Daily Beast in 2012. “I think people should do whatever they want as long as they don’t hurt anyone or intrude on anybody else.”

Joseph Richard Redner was born on July 2, 1940, in Hackensack, N.J. After his father, William Redner, left the family when Joe was a young child, his mother, Agnes (Statella) Redner, moved with him and his brother, William, to Tampa, where she waited on tables.

Joe dropped out of high school at 16 and spent several years working odd jobs in shops and warehouses. For a while, he traveled with a carnival.

In 1972, one of his employers, impressed by his work ethic, asked him to manage a go-go club, the Deep South. Mr. Redner began looking for ways to expand the business, adding more dancers and promoting ever-more-risqué performances.

After the Supreme Court ruled in a series of cases that nudity on film could be considered speech, and was therefore protected under the First Amendment, Mr. Redner decided to test to see whether that ruling covered live performance as well.

Though the Supreme Court ruling did open the door for nudity in adult clubs, cities like Tampa fought back with tight restrictions on where and how they could operate. Mr. Redner found himself spending almost as much time in zoning meetings and courtroom hearings as he did at his club.

He finally opened his first fully nude strip club, the Night Gallery, in 1976. Later, he added other clubs in and around Tampa, culminating with Mons Venus in 1982. While the other clubs eventually closed, Mons remained his flagship.

Mr. Redner developed a reputation with Tampa-area dancers for running an enlightened business: They did not have to pay kickbacks or perform in private rooms, and set their own hours.

And because he believed that the job of manager attracted the wrong kind of man, he mostly hired women to oversee his clubs.

“I think they have more compassion and common sense than men do,” he told The Tampa Bay Times in 2022.

Mr. Redner’s marriage to Lorelei Jackson ended in divorce, but they remained close friends.

Along with his son, he is survived by three daughters, Teresa Redner, Joy Lynn Redner and Angela Smith; his longtime companion, Edie Burns, and her son, Kyle; and 11 grandchildren. His brother died in 2016, and his daughter Reyline Harris died in 2017.

Mr. Redner sold Mons Venus last year, but stayed on as a consultant. It remains one of the most popular adult clubs in the country.

“Sex is a very strong attraction,” he told The St. Petersburg Times in 1999. “I didn’t make it strong; nature made it strong.”

item.title: The New Worst-Case Scenario for Election Officials: Federal Interference
item.description:
State and local elections officials regularly plan for floods, fires and computer glitches.

This year, they are teaching poll workers what to do if immigration enforcement officers show up. They are drilling them about the statute that bars federal agents from voting places. They are running through the limits of what federal monitors may and may not do on Election Day.

Much of the preparations for Nov. 3 can be distilled into one overarching concern — that the Trump administration will somehow attempt to meddle with the voting process or the results. The tricky part, officials said, is predicting what shape that interference might take while also recognizing that it might not materialize at all.

“This is the first time ever that we have had to engage in scenario planning to safeguard against potential federal interference in elections,” said Shenna Bellows, the secretary of state in Maine. “It seems like the federal government is now adversarial to the states.”

It remains to be seen whether any of these scenarios will play out. Many federal officials have dismissed the idea that agents or soldiers could be sent to the polls, and the courts have blocked most of President Trump’s efforts to insert the federal government into state and local election administration.

And some of the country’s most prominent voting advocates have sought to assure the public that election administrators are well-prepared to protect the vote. David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department, said the most chilling possibilities are unlikely to come to pass because the courts would likely block them.

“But election officials feel more comfortable to know they’ve thought about this, and discussed it,” said Mr. Becker, who runs the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to support election officials in both parties.

Even so, the Trump Administration has already taken significant steps to try to shape the voting process this year. Mr. Trump has sought to sow doubt about the security of elections. His administration has demanded that states turn over voter lists, and has tried unsuccessfully to change mail voting rules. Last week, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to pre-emptively block the certification of the Senate race there if the Republican candidate loses by a narrow margin.

With one week until Election Day, officials around the country say that they are bracing for even more unwanted and potentially undemocratic federal intervention — even as they can’t be sure what, if anything, the Trump Administration might do. To prepare, secretaries of state and other state and local officials have met with lawyers and local law enforcement agencies, trained poll workers and held meetings to consider what could come next.

Among their top concerns: that Mr. Trump’s attacks on the integrity of American voting systems could form the basis for challenging the legitimacy of the results. Along with that unease comes the worry that any federal intervention could further undermine public confidence in elections and cause voters to stay home.

The next step is a guessing game, they said.

Could federal officials try to seize ballots, as they did earlier this year in Fulton County, Ga., as part of a criminal investigation that thus far hasn’t resulted in any charges?

Could Mr. Trump deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel or other federal agents to polling sites, even though his homeland security chief has said I.C.E. will not patrol polling stations and would be deployed to such an area only to investigate “specific threats?”

Might he invoke the Insurrection Act and somehow summon the military in connection with the election? Mr. Trump has refused to rule out the possibility.

“We really are shadowboxing here, because we don’t know when or if the blow is going to land,” said Steve Simon, the Minnesota secretary of state. “We don’t know the character of, or content of, what might be headed our way.”

Mr. Trump, who has long claimed without proof that U.S. elections are rigged, sought to overturn his 2020 election loss. Earlier this year, he said the federal government should “get involved” in elections, even though the Constitution empowers the states and Congress — not the executive branch — to govern elections.

Ms. Bellows and Mr. Simon are Democrats. But Republican election officials have also planned for the possibility of federal intervention. Deidre Henderson, the lieutenant governor of Utah and a Republican, recently said that while she did not “necessarily expect” such interference, officials in her state were still planning for it.

In a statement, Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said the bipartisan concerns about election interference were unfounded.

“The only ‘worries’ about election security are caused by radical Democrats who refuse to enact basic election security measures, supported by the majority of Americans, including voter ID and citizenship verification to ensure only Americans are electing America’s leaders,” Ms. Bis said. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”

Several voting advocacy groups have offered training and advice to election officials to help them get ready. One organization, the Government Counsel and Election Officials Network, explains to election administrators the legal basics that could be helpful in the case of federal action, whether civil or criminal, such as the seizure of machines or documents.

The group’s website provides samples of what federal grand jury subpoenas and search warrants look like. It also advises how to respond to a federal investigation, including what to do when agents show up with a search warrant.

“Step 1,” the site says: “Stay calm.”

Tina Barton, the co-chairwoman of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, said her team has helped run about 140 training sessions for officials with local government and law enforcement this year, up from 67 such sessions in 2024.

Some of those officials, including law enforcement leaders in Northern Virginia, said they were concerned about how immigration enforcement might affect the election process. Although Mr. Trump’s homeland security chief has said ICE will not patrol polling stations, Ms. Barton said that some congressional officials nonetheless expressed concern about the possibility. She said she helped lead a training scenario in which ICE enforcement was near a polling location.

Ms. Bellows, the Maine secretary of state, said her team introduced a new slide this year into its training presentation for law enforcement. It provides the text of the federal statute that bars armed federal agents from polling places.

“It’s sad that we’re in this posture,” Ms. Bellows said in a phone interview. “But it’s just the way it is in 2026, given the administration’s rhetoric, and their actions.”

Barb Byrum, the clerk of Ingham County, Mich., said she was already concerned by some actions of the Trump administration, including the Justice Department’s deployment of federal election monitors to her county during the August primary. She said it was the first such deployment of federal monitors to her county in her nearly 14 years as clerk.

“The feds suggested that there were long lines, voters were not offered provisional ballots and clerks and precinct workers failed to use the qualified voter file to check voters,” she said. “All of which is simply not true.”

After the primary, Ms. Byrum put her election workers through additional training on what federal monitors were and were not permitted to do under state law.

“They can watch the process,” Ms. Byrum said. “They can’t touch anything, they can’t ask any questions. They can literally just watch — monitor.”

Ms. Byrum said she found it disheartening that she now considered the federal government a potential threat to the election.

Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University, formerly worked on voting rights for the Biden administration. He said nearly everywhere across the country, Justice Department observers must adhere to the same rules of behavior at polling places as any other member of the public.

Earlier this week, Dana Nessel, the Michigan attorney general, said the Justice Department’s civil rights division had sent notices to seven Michigan municipalities that election monitors from the department would come to their polling places on Election Day. In a statement, Ms. Nessel, a Democrat, sought to quell anxiety about the plans.

“It’s important for residents know that D.O.J. monitors are a standard part of our election process, and we anticipate they will comport with state and federal law,” she said.

Some officials are hesitant to share granular details of their preparations, for fear of giving the federal government a tactical advantage if legal skirmishes arise.

For Democrats, the politics of discussing preparations are also complicated. By having an open discussion about pre-election planning, they said, they show their constituents that they are taking the threats seriously. But they also recognize that such discussions could intimidate voters from going to the polls.

In an interview, Keith Ellison, Minnesota’s attorney general and a Democrat, said he and Mr. Simon, the secretary of state, have been working in tandem to prepare for election threats.

Asked how concerned he was about the threats to the Nov. 3 election on a scale of 1 to 10, Mr. Ellison said: “I’m at a seven.” He added: “It’s as high as it’s ever been for me.”

During a recent online forum, Lisa Lyons, the clerk and registrar of deeds in Kent County, Mich., said her staff regularly communicated with her government’s legal team about potential troubles.

“We’re going to follow the law,” she said. “We’re going to follow the Constitution. We’re going to protect our election equipment.”
